nodes.label: The business owner (referred to as Ben in the transcript) operates an info-consu…
nodes.description:
**Example:** The business owner (referred to as Ben in the transcript) operates an info-consulting business based in Argentina generating $300K/month revenue at 80% margins (~$240K/month profit) through Instagram organic short-form content. The funnel works as follows: reels and stories drive followers to claim lead magnets, starting DM conversations; DM setters then book calls from those conversations; booked calls go to a thank-you page with a video before connecting to a closer. Despite 20,000+ leads/month (700/day), only 20 calls are booked per day and only 10 show up, resulting in 80 closed clients per month — a 0.3% lead-to-client conversion rate. Hormozi identifies DM setter headcount (not show rate, not qualification rate, not closer capacity) as the binding constraint and recommends hiring approximately 10 DM setters to work all incoming leads.

_from 300k_month_with_80_margins_on_instagram_organic_g2i-aBfWfvA.txt_

nodes.label: During a live coaching call, Alex Hormozi worked with a luxury wedding entertain…
nodes.description:
**Example:** During a live coaching call, Alex Hormozi worked with a luxury wedding entertainment business owner named Mike whose hybrid DJ-band concept was priced at $10K-$30K. Hormozi immediately flagged that $10K felt like the cost of napkins at a luxury wedding and that the price was incongruent with the luxury positioning. He proposed adding a $100K option on the spot, arguing that $100K would become the bread-and-butter price point and that a $250K ultra-premium tier would be needed to serve ultra-high-net-worth clients (e.g., a hedge fund manager paying for a child's wedding). Mike confirmed that prospects who saw pricing in advance self-canceled, which Hormozi diagnosed as a qualification failure at the opt-in stage rather than a pricing or sales execution problem.

_from 30k_isn_t_luxury_it_s_cheap_Zk3xE-0jFZc.txt_

nodes.label: Hormozi walked Mike through a specific two-tier anchor upsell structure for the …
nodes.description:
**Example:** Hormozi walked Mike through a specific two-tier anchor upsell structure for the luxury wedding entertainment business. The new offer structure would be: (1) present the $100K package as the primary offer and sell it fully, identifying one high-end feature that only the most elite buyers need; (2) if the prospect declines, offer the $35K package (the current $30K offer, slightly raised) by saying the $100K includes a specific premium element they may not need, and if they do not need it, the $35K package covers 90% of the same experience. Hormozi estimated 10%-30% of buyers would purchase at $100K and the rest would concentrate on the $35K tier, roughly doubling average transaction value.

_from 30k_isn_t_luxury_it_s_cheap_Zk3xE-0jFZc.txt_

nodes.label: Hormozi described a VSL viewing verification tactic: after the prospect says the…
nodes.description:
**Example:** Hormozi described a VSL viewing verification tactic: after the prospect says they prefer to watch the VSL alone (rather than together on the call), embed a secret word or compliance cue (e.g., 'text us the head count for your wedding') inside the video. When the prospect texts back the number, the seller knows they watched. If they did not text back, the seller has a natural opener on the call: 'Did you get a chance to watch the video?' This tactic ensures that every prospect who reaches the sales call has been pre-framed by the VSL content, reducing the time spent re-explaining context.

_from 30k_isn_t_luxury_it_s_cheap_Zk3xE-0jFZc.txt_

nodes.label: A med-spa owner presented her situation: $3M revenue, ~$700K net profit, $200K m…
nodes.plugin: Owner Delivery Time as Scaling Constraint
nodes.description:
**Example:** A med-spa owner presented her situation: $3M revenue, ~$700K net profit, $200K medical director salary (total owner take ~$1M). She wanted to reach $20M through multiple locations within two to five years. When asked what was stopping her, she said bandwidth. Alex Hormozi quickly established that with 30% margins the constraint was not money; she confirmed 80% of her time was clinical work leaving 20% for business. Hormozi's diagnosis: hire a replacement physician at ~$200K (redirecting her existing medical director draw), reclaim 80% of her time, and use that bandwidth to scale locations. The sales issues she perceived as a constraint were secondary because fixing them would only add ~$300K in profit, which she acknowledged would not materially change her life or situation.

**Example:** Supreme Power Wash (power washing, solar panel cleaning, window cleaning) generates $500K revenue and $250K profit annually, with primary customer acquisition via door knocking (~20-25 deals/month at $350-$1,800 average, roughly $500 blended) and referrals. The owner is spending $2,000/month on ads but cannot confirm how many customers come from ads versus door knocking. Alex Hormozi uses this case to illustrate the attribution gap: the owner suspects ads work but has no data, so neither scaling ads nor cutting them is defensible.

_from 500k_power_washing_business_stuck_on_referrals_gRQLYWfwRIA.txt_

nodes.label: When the Supreme Power Wash owner explained a desire to shift from residential t…
nodes.description:
**Example:** When the Supreme Power Wash owner explained a desire to shift from residential to commercial B2B recurring clients (citing one commercial client that brought higher recurring revenue), Alex Hormozi reframed the goal: instead of opening a new channel and new avatar simultaneously, the owner should first get attribution on the existing $2,000/month paid channel, verify it produces positive ROI, scale it to $4,000 or $6,000, and only then consider commercial. The one commercial client already in the portfolio was a proof-of-concept example, not a signal to abandon residential.

_from 500k_power_washing_business_stuck_on_referrals_gRQLYWfwRIA.txt_

nodes.label: Alex Hormozi describes declining to endorse a book for a relatively prominent pe…
nodes.description:
**Example:** Alex Hormozi describes declining to endorse a book for a relatively prominent person who reached out to him. Rather than ghosting the request or giving a vague yes he would not honor, he wrote a message saying he respected the person too much to give a half-hearted answer, that he would not endorse the book, but that the person could send it and he would likely skim it given other reading priorities. Before sending, he reasoned through the second-order consequence: ghosting would produce a slight negative impression with a null outcome; a truthful polite decline would signal that his yes, when given in future, carries real weight. The example illustrates the two-moves-ahead consequence analysis claim.

_from a_lifetime_of_personal_development_in_18_minutes_PsxOnxIU274.txt_

nodes.label: Alex Hormozi describes a conversation with one of his portfolio CEOs who was exp…
nodes.description:
**Example:** Alex Hormozi describes a conversation with one of his portfolio CEOs who was experiencing stress. He used the Yeti can analogy to explain the emotion-action gap: a Yeti vacuum-insulated can has its internal temperature on one side and external temperature on the other, with a vacuum between them. The desired state for the CEO was to behave as though they had that vacuum — feelings on one side, behavior on the other, with deliberate space as the insulating layer. This illustrates the Emotion-Action Decoupling framework.

_from a_lifetime_of_personal_development_in_18_minutes_PsxOnxIU274.txt_

nodes.label: Alex Hormozi cites B.F. Skinner's maxim that the common saying 'you can lead a h…
nodes.description:
**Example:** Alex Hormozi cites B.F. Skinner's maxim that the common saying 'you can lead a horse to water but you can't make it drink' is false. Skinner argues that by dehydrating the horse, salting its mouth, placing it in heat, and positioning its face one inch from water, one can near-guarantee that it will drink. Hormozi uses this example to illustrate that environmental condition stacking makes a target behavior essentially inevitable without requiring willpower from the agent.

_from a_lifetime_of_personal_development_in_18_minutes_PsxOnxIU274.txt_

nodes.label: Alex Hormozi illustrates the good/bad valence claim with the parable of the old …
nodes.description:
**Example:** Alex Hormozi illustrates the good/bad valence claim with the parable of the old man and the horse: a father gives his son a horse, and the villagers say this is wonderful; the old man says 'we'll see.' The son breaks his leg riding the horse; the villagers say this is terrible; the old man says 'we'll see.' When the army comes to conscript young men, the son cannot go because of his broken leg; the villagers say this is wonderful; the old man again says 'we'll see.' The story illustrates that the downstream consequences of any event are unknowable at the time of occurrence, making any in-moment good/bad judgment premature.

_from a_lifetime_of_personal_development_in_18_minutes_PsxOnxIU274.txt_

nodes.label: Alex Hormozi describes the events of the morning of September 11, 2001. A man's …
nodes.description:
**Example:** Alex Hormozi describes the events of the morning of September 11, 2001. A man's colleague gifted him an illustrated tie for his birthday. His shirt clashed with it, but the colleague insisted he wear it because it would make him feel confident. He returned to his hotel to change while she went to the North Tower, where she died. He survived. Hormozi uses this to illustrate that one cannot assign a good or bad valuation to an action — giving that tie was neither good nor bad — because the downstream consequences are unknowable.

_from a_lifetime_of_personal_development_in_18_minutes_PsxOnxIU274.txt_

nodes.label: Alex Hormozi describes a podcaster he knows who snapped his Achilles tendon and …
nodes.description:
**Example:** Alex Hormozi describes a podcaster he knows who snapped his Achilles tendon and could barely walk. During the recovery period, the man decided he might as well start the podcast he had been meaning to launch. Years later, the podcast became a top-50 podcast in the world. Hormozi uses this as the canonical illustration of the reframing question: what would make this the best thing that ever happened to you? In this case, the forced inactivity from a negative physical event directly enabled a career outcome that would not have occurred otherwise.

_from a_lifetime_of_personal_development_in_18_minutes_PsxOnxIU274.txt_

nodes.label: A 17-year-old asked for advice on starting a pool construction business, noting …
nodes.description:
**Example:** A 17-year-old asked for advice on starting a pool construction business, noting his father holds a construction license in Florida and that he had done digital marketing for a pool company for a year. Alex Hormozi responded with a complete four-step playbook: run $5,000/month in PPC, call every lead within 60 seconds, sell a $1,500 upfront package, then roll the customer immediately into a continuity offering. The advice treats PPC + fast response + upfront capture + continuity sequencing as the minimum viable go-to-market for a new local service business.

_from advice_to_a_17_year_old_starting_a_business_Hw1W8G6idMY.txt_

The argument is that $2,000 falls below the threshold where the financial reward overrides the activation friction, while $6,000-$10,000 crosses it for a business owner whose time is valuable.

_from affiliate_offer_10x_the_kickback_to_boost_referrals_dX-eI11-kSw.txt_

**Example:** Hormozi uses a concrete agency math example to justify cold-acquiring agency affiliates via ads: an e-commerce agency with 30 clients that does a webinar and converts half would refer 15 clients. At $6,000 per closed deal, that agency earns $90,000 in a single month. Hormozi notes this creates a powerful affiliate testimonial that can itself be used to recruit further affiliates.

_from affiliate_offer_10x_the_kickback_to_boost_referrals_dX-eI11-kSw.txt_

nodes.label: To illustrate the ease-of-activation lever, Hormozi describes the full handholdi…

**Example:** To illustrate the ease-of-activation lever, Hormozi describes the full handholding package: pre-written emails (built with AI assistance), a custom-branded landing page, and sending a team member to plug everything into the affiliate's CRM. The framing is that the affiliate has zero tasks remaining after agreeing to the program.

_from affiliate_offer_10x_the_kickback_to_boost_referrals_dX-eI11-kSw.txt_

nodes.label: Alex Hormozi describes his first gym: a mentor had built his business on flyer d…
nodes.description:
**Example:** Alex Hormozi describes his first gym: a mentor had built his business on flyer distribution, so Hormozi distributed 300 flyers and waited two weeks. One call came in — someone complaining he had dinged their Mercedes. When his mentor followed up and asked about the test size, Hormozi said 300 total. The mentor said that was too small to tell anything; his own practice was 5,000 flyers per batch to find a winner, then 5,000 per day at scale — roughly 150,000 per month. The story illustrates that Hormozi interpreted the absence of response as proof the channel failed, when in fact he had not run a statistically meaningful test.

_from are_you_even_trying__deYfX6flgo.txt_

nodes.label: Alex Hormozi compares a new salesperson with 90 days of experience (roughly 400-…
nodes.description:
**Example:** Alex Hormozi compares a new salesperson with 90 days of experience (roughly 400-500 live calls, fewer closed deals) to John, a top rep who has closed 4,000 deals — implying John has taken roughly 12,000+ calls. The new rep wonders why John is better; Hormozi's answer is simply volume: John has closed 10x as many deals and taken ~30x as many calls. The comparison illustrates that skill gaps between beginners and experts are driven not by talent but by cumulative reps.

_from are_you_even_trying__deYfX6flgo.txt_

nodes.label: Alex Hormozi uses his own content operation as a benchmark: his team produces 45…
nodes.description:
**Example:** Alex Hormozi uses his own content operation as a benchmark: his team produces 450 pieces of content per week, with Twitter (X) as the primary hub from which everything is generated. A creator who posts once per day for 90 days (90 posts) would statistically be in the top 1% of creators by persistence — yet Hormozi's team produces that same 90 posts in roughly two days. The example demonstrates that what feels like exceptional effort to a beginner is, from the top performer's vantage point, a rounding error.

_from are_you_even_trying__deYfX6flgo.txt_

nodes.label: Rory Sutherland describes rebranding the Silverlink Metro railway (later called …
nodes.plugin: Undefined Words Create Mythology and Prevent Clear Thinking
nodes.description:
**Example:** Rory Sutherland describes rebranding the Silverlink Metro railway (later called the Overground) and adding it to the London Tube map. For the roughly 40 years the line existed as Silverlink Metro, usage was negligible. Within six months of rebranding it as the Overground and placing it on the Tube map, usage more than doubled. The line itself was unchanged; only the map representation changed. Sutherland uses this to illustrate how a mental model (the Tube map) determines what people perceive as existing, and how adding something to the dominant map can instantaneously double its utilisation.

_from artificial_intelligence_vs_human_intelligence_2015_archives_n0owiLU4EW8.txt_

nodes.label: Rory Sutherland describes the M20/M25 junction near Dover as a road sign design …
nodes.description:
**Example:** Rory Sutherland describes the M20/M25 junction near Dover as a road sign design that systematically causes drivers to miss the M25 turnoff: the first sign mentions London on both sides and gives no distance to the junction; a second sign appears on the horizon, causing drivers to defer their decision; but before the second sign is reached, the junction passes. Sutherland says he made this mistake five times before realising it was a design flaw, not driver error, and confirmed it via Google Street View.

_from artificial_intelligence_vs_human_intelligence_2015_archives_n0owiLU4EW8.txt_

nodes.label: Rory Sutherland describes a restaurant wine-service system as a sustained contex…
nodes.description:
**Example:** Rory Sutherland describes a restaurant wine-service system as a sustained contextual architecture that drives wine consumption: wine glasses are pre-set on tables, the menu is called a 'wine list' not a 'drinks list', the wine list is eight pages versus one back page for spirits, it is handed to one person who must choose for the whole table, and staff refill glasses mid-meal without being asked. Each element removes gin or spirits as a live option without prohibiting it, and the refill convention is perceived as service rather than consumption pressure. He uses this to show how context shapes choice invisibly.

_from artificial_intelligence_vs_human_intelligence_2015_archives_n0owiLU4EW8.txt_

nodes.label: Rory Sutherland describes placing a wall clock in a FedEx print ad — cited as re…
nodes.description:
**Example:** Rory Sutherland describes placing a wall clock in a FedEx print ad — cited as research by a South African behavioural scientist — where nearly all readers were unaware of the clock consciously, yet the ad with the clock was more than twice as likely to evoke the concept of speedy service compared to the ad without the clock. He uses this to illustrate that System 1 processes contextual cues we do not consciously register.

_from artificial_intelligence_vs_human_intelligence_2015_archives_n0owiLU4EW8.txt_

nodes.label: Rory Sutherland describes the footprint illusion: two sets of footprints are sho…
nodes.description:
**Example:** Rory Sutherland describes the footprint illusion: two sets of footprints are shown side by side, one appearing convex and one concave. When rotated, they are revealed to be identical photographs. The brain applies a statistical prior (light comes from above) to determine convexity; flipping the image flips the percept. He uses this to demonstrate that the brain is an inference engine applying priors, not an objective image processor.

_from artificial_intelligence_vs_human_intelligence_2015_archives_n0owiLU4EW8.txt_

nodes.label: Rory Sutherland describes the Nespresso pricing frame: if Nespresso coffee were …
nodes.description:
**Example:** Rory Sutherland describes the Nespresso pricing frame: if Nespresso coffee were sold in a large jar like Nescafe, the equivalent cost (~£50) would appear prohibitive. Sold instead as individual pods at 29p each, the relevant comparison shifts from a jar of instant coffee to a Starbucks cup at £2.40 — making the pod feel economical. The physical and commercial format of the product determines the anchor against which price is judged, not the absolute price level.

_from artificial_intelligence_vs_human_intelligence_2015_archives_n0owiLU4EW8.txt_

nodes.label: Rory Sutherland makes the analogy of a friend who owns a racehorse: if the frien…
nodes.description:
**Example:** Rory Sutherland makes the analogy of a friend who owns a racehorse: if the friend says 'I think my horse will win on Saturday' verbally to people in a pub, that information is nearly worthless because everyone says that. If the same friend goes to a bookmaker and bets £10,000 on the horse to win, the same information acquires a totally different character — because the bettor is now exposed to real loss from being wrong. Sutherland uses this to illustrate costly signalling: the information is identical, but the commitment attached to it makes it credible.

_from artificial_intelligence_vs_human_intelligence_2015_archives_n0owiLU4EW8.txt_

nodes.label: Rory Sutherland described his own career as an illustration of the value of non-…
nodes.description:
**Example:** Rory Sutherland described his own career as an illustration of the value of non-linear early-stage paths: he read Classics at Christ College, joined Ogilvy in 1988 as a graduate trainee and was named the worst graduate trainee the agency had ever hired, was fired from the planning department, reapplied, was sent to creative, became a copywriter, and five years later was executive creative director of Ogilvy One, eventually becoming vice chairman of Ogilvy UK. He notes that even time spent as a poor account person remained of value to him decades later, and that a messy early career should carry no shame.

_from be_good_at_two_things_feat_rory_sutherland_vice_chairman_of_YlsQkllMQN8.txt_

nodes.label: Rory Sutherland used the Pepsi-Kylie Jenner advertisement (circa 2017) to illust…
nodes.description:
**Example:** Rory Sutherland used the Pepsi-Kylie Jenner advertisement (circa 2017) to illustrate the dynamics of issue-based advertising and social media outrage. The advertising industry largely identified the ad's problems immediately; outside the industry, most people saw nothing wrong with it. He argued the ad's failure was that strategic intent was visible ('strategic bra straps showing') without earning the credibility to carry that intent, and that the mainstream media then amplified the minority outrage from Twitter into a nationwide scandal.

_from be_good_at_two_things_feat_rory_sutherland_vice_chairman_of_YlsQkllMQN8.txt_

nodes.label: Rory Sutherland noted that pre-social-media investigative journalism required jo…
nodes.description:
**Example:** Rory Sutherland noted that pre-social-media investigative journalism required journalists to physically locate and interview members of the public, which made extreme outlier opinions difficult to source because such people were genuinely rare and geographically dispersed. On Twitter, a journalist seeking outrage about an advertisement can simply search for aggrieved users within minutes and cut-paste their comments into an article, transforming a fringe position into apparent mainstream sentiment.

_from be_good_at_two_things_feat_rory_sutherland_vice_chairman_of_YlsQkllMQN8.txt_

nodes.label: Alex Hormozi described his own book launch as an illustrative counterexample of …
nodes.description:
**Example:** Alex Hormozi described his own book launch as an illustrative counterexample of warm vs. cold process mismatch. At the book launch, he had a warm audience who already knew him. He could have sent a simple email saying he wrote 17 extra chapters and offering them free with an AI bundle — and estimated he would have converted roughly one-third of sales from that email alone to a warm list. But if he had treated his entire audience (including cold segments) with that same minimal-context email approach, he would have under-converted by approximately two-thirds of what he should have achieved. The warm shortcut only works on the warm slice.

_from booking_100_calls_a_month_but_closing_half_Tk0e0z8h64Y.txt_

nodes.label: The video testimonial agency in the conversation was at $6M in revenue, selling …
nodes.description:
**Example:** The video testimonial agency in the conversation was at $6M in revenue, selling to mid-market and enterprise B2B software companies (director of marketing level), with a $15K average order value. They had grown historically through inbound and word-of-mouth (high close rates, buyers already in buying cycle). They had recently shifted to cold outbound via LinkedIn ads targeting named accounts, booking 100 calls per month. Of those, 85% showed up. But the close rate was only 6% of total leads booked (approximately 8% of shows). Alex Hormozi identified the root cause immediately as applying the same sales process they used on warm inbound leads to these cold outbound calls, without adding a VSL pre-frame, qualification script, or sales training cadence.

_from booking_100_calls_a_month_but_closing_half_Tk0e0z8h64Y.txt_

nodes.label: Alex Hormozi cited his general counsel as a real-world example of the continued-…
nodes.description:
**Example:** Alex Hormozi cited his general counsel as a real-world example of the continued-education subscription model in professional services. She is enrolled in a $3,000-per-year attorney forum that provides regulatory updates and allows members to ask questions of subject-matter experts. Hormozi used this to illustrate that the annual-subscription continued-education model is proven and common in licensed professions, and that a similar structure could work for Brazilian accountants.

_from brazil_s_accounting_empire_12m_revenue_1_decision_left_hbRuTx98gM0.txt_

nodes.label: Hormozi used the CRM integration scenario as a concrete example of net negative …
nodes.description:
**Example:** Hormozi used the CRM integration scenario as a concrete example of net negative churn: if 100 accountants subscribe to an accounting software CRM and 20 cancel over the year, the remaining 80 grow their businesses and upgrade to higher tiers, so total revenue from the surviving cohort exceeds the starting-year total. He used this to illustrate why deeply integrated software retains more than 100% of revenue even with meaningful churn.

_from brazil_s_accounting_empire_12m_revenue_1_decision_left_hbRuTx98gM0.txt_

nodes.label: Rory Sutherland recounts landing at an airport where a pilot announced they coul…
nodes.description:
**Example:** Rory Sutherland recounts landing at an airport where a pilot announced they could not use an air bridge because a plane was blocking the gate, but framed the bus as getting passengers directly to passport control — so they would not need to carry bags as far. The audience's evaluation of the bus shifted from inconvenient (a way to reach the airport) to convenient (a way to reach passport control without walking). The same conveyance, the same journey, produced opposite appraisals depending on which endpoint was made salient.

_from bring_back_the_green_cross_code_rory_sutherland_vice_chairma_6CBqGsAdFa8.txt_

nodes.label: Rory Sutherland describes the Avis We're No. 2, So We Try Harder campaign as an …
nodes.description:
**Example:** Rory Sutherland describes the Avis We're No. 2, So We Try Harder campaign as an advertising case where being smaller than Hertz — normally a disadvantage in the car-hire context — was reframed as evidence of greater effort and customer focus. Four words added under what was effectively an ad for Hertz converted it into a compelling claim for Avis.

_from bring_back_the_green_cross_code_rory_sutherland_vice_chairma_6CBqGsAdFa8.txt_

nodes.label: Rory Sutherland describes the rise of veganism as an example of how a 10-15% min…
nodes.description:
**Example:** Rory Sutherland describes the rise of veganism as an example of how a 10-15% minority changed infrastructure: once vegan demand reached a critical mass, every catering event and restaurant menu had to add a vegan option, which then made subsequent adoption progressively easier. Early vegetarians had one unappealing option; as the minority grew, the entire choice architecture transformed.

_from bring_back_the_green_cross_code_rory_sutherland_vice_chairma_6CBqGsAdFa8.txt_

nodes.label: Rory Sutherland cites the London Tube map's impact on property markets: after de…
nodes.description:
**Example:** Rory Sutherland cites the London Tube map's impact on property markets: after decades of people using the map to buy homes near tube stations, station-adjacent properties became overvalued. A friend moving from Fulham (tube-adjacent) to Herne Hill (not on the tube, and with Hill in the name) discovered the commute took half as long — because the tube map had completely distorted their sense of distance and priority.

_from bring_back_the_green_cross_code_rory_sutherland_vice_chairma_6CBqGsAdFa8.txt_

nodes.label: Rory Sutherland describes a pizza delivery app experiment: both the website and …
nodes.description:
**Example:** Rory Sutherland describes a pizza delivery app experiment: both the website and app defaulted to ASAP delivery, and phone orders were never asked when they wanted delivery unless the customer volunteered a delayed time. When the app's default was changed to a time-of-day selector, delivery windows stretched to approximately one hour without loss of sales, and customer satisfaction rose by approximately 50%, because waiting with a known arrival time felt better than rushing with uncertainty.

_from bring_back_the_green_cross_code_rory_sutherland_vice_chairma_6CBqGsAdFa8.txt_

nodes.label: Rory Sutherland recounts wanting to install an EV home charger before buying an …
nodes.description:
**Example:** Rory Sutherland recounts wanting to install an EV home charger before buying an electric car but being told by the subsidy program that he needed to prove ownership of an electric car first. His argument: selling someone a charger achieves the policy goal, because a person who has installed a home charger would feel irrational buying a petrol car afterwards. The catch-22 design of the scheme illustrates how persuasion logic (commitment device) is structurally absent from policy implementation.

_from bring_back_the_green_cross_code_rory_sutherland_vice_chairma_6CBqGsAdFa8.txt_

nodes.label: Rory Sutherland describes the TV color example: an expensive 4K television that …
nodes.description:
**Example:** Rory Sutherland describes the TV color example: an expensive 4K television that promises a billion colors actually produces only three primary colors (red, green, blue). All color mixing happens in the visual cortex — the brain synthesizes colors including magenta, which does not exist in the physical spectrum, because the brain cannot distinguish equal inputs of red-green and invents a color to explain the absence of green. This illustrates the broader point that psychology can generate perceptual value (a billion colors) from minimal physical inputs (three color channels).

_from bring_back_the_green_cross_code_rory_sutherland_vice_chairma_6CBqGsAdFa8.txt_

nodes.label: Rory Sutherland explains the Beyond Meat brand positioning: nearly all previous …
nodes.description:
**Example:** Rory Sutherland explains the Beyond Meat brand positioning: nearly all previous vegetarian food was framed around sacrifice and self-denial. Beyond Meat instead positioned its product as self-indulgent — meatier than meat itself. This contrasts with the hair-shirt framing of earlier vegetarian brands and illustrates how removing the self-denial signal can unlock mass-market adoption that counter-signaling approaches could not achieve.

_from bring_back_the_green_cross_code_rory_sutherland_vice_chairma_6CBqGsAdFa8.txt_

nodes.label: Rory Sutherland observes that the most common tourist journey in London is Leice…
nodes.description:
**Example:** Rory Sutherland observes that the most common tourist journey in London is Leicester Square to Covent Garden on the Tube, a distance so short that a tennis ball could be thrown between the stations above ground. Tourists use the tube for this journey because the map makes the connection visually salient, while the walkable distance is invisible. The Central line is similarly overused because it runs left-to-right in a straight line on the map; the Victoria line — described by Sutherland as like teleportation — is significantly underused because it appears wiggly and cognitively difficult to follow.

_from bring_back_the_green_cross_code_rory_sutherland_vice_chairma_6CBqGsAdFa8.txt_

nodes.label: Rory Sutherland observes that in China some households own large plasma televisi…
nodes.description:
**Example:** Rory Sutherland observes that in China some households own large plasma televisions before having indoor plumbing, which he uses to illustrate that collective goods (sewage) require coordinated public expenditure while individual goods (televisions) can be procured unilaterally. This frames the tax-as-burden narrative critique: some expenditure is genuinely better done collectively, and the tax-relief framing pre-empts that reasoning.

_from bring_back_the_green_cross_code_rory_sutherland_vice_chairma_6CBqGsAdFa8.txt_

nodes.label: Alex Hormozi contrasts two archetypes to illustrate the four-component model in …
nodes.description:
**Example:** Alex Hormozi contrasts two archetypes to illustrate the four-component model in operation. The maximally mentally tough person is almost impossible to disrupt (huge tolerance), barely shifts behavior when they are disrupted (high fortitude, imperceptible change), returns to baseline almost immediately (high resilience), and uses every hard experience to reach a higher new baseline (high adaptability). The result is continuous improvement. The opposite archetype—what Hormozi calls a mental weenie—is sent spiraling by trivial events like slow Wi-Fi (low tolerance), changes behavior dramatically in response (low fortitude), stays in the degraded state for an extended period replaying the triggering moment (low resilience), and permanently worsens as a result (low adaptability). The visual contrast makes each component discrete and observable.

_from build_a_mind_so_strong_it_scares_people_SE9_1PYsaP0.txt_

nodes.label: Alex Hormozi described writing the mental toughness framework in the aftermath o…
nodes.description:
**Example:** Alex Hormozi described writing the mental toughness framework in the aftermath of his mother’s death. He stated he wanted to understand the feelings he was going through and the behavioral changes they produced, asking himself how the experience could make him better rather than worse. He noted the culturally uncomfortable nature of asking how to improve from a parent’s death, but argued that the deceased would not want him to be permanently worse as a result. This personal context illustrates the adaptability component: reframing grief not as a permanent downward shift in baseline but as a forcing function for growth.

_from build_a_mind_so_strong_it_scares_people_SE9_1PYsaP0.txt_

nodes.label: Alex Hormozi referenced Viktor Frankl’s Man’s Search for Meaning to illustrate t…
nodes.description:
**Example:** Alex Hormozi referenced Viktor Frankl’s Man’s Search for Meaning to illustrate the gap between stimulus and response where volitional behavior choice exists. Frankl’s observation—derived from surviving Nazi concentration camps—is that even in conditions of extreme adversity, a person retains the ability to choose their response in the moment between what happens to them and how they react. Hormozi used this to ground the claim that behavioral self-determination is not merely aspirational but documented under conditions far harsher than ordinary life setbacks.

_from build_a_mind_so_strong_it_scares_people_SE9_1PYsaP0.txt_

nodes.label: Hormozi used the movie-protagonist frame to illustrate adaptability: imagine wak…
nodes.description:
**Example:** Hormozi used the movie-protagonist frame to illustrate adaptability: imagine waking up as the main character in a movie you know has a happy ending. The character loses the promotion, does not get the romantic partner, and loses someone they love—yet the audience knows the story resolves well. What would that character do next to move the plot forward? Hormozi argued that as soon as you can answer that question, you do it. The frame collapses the perceived gap between bad circumstances and growth-oriented action by making the growth action narratively obvious rather than emotionally forced.

_from build_a_mind_so_strong_it_scares_people_SE9_1PYsaP0.txt_

nodes.label: Joel McDonald's travel-hedging business (Just Get Out of Town, $6.4M trailing-12…
nodes.description:
**Example:** Joel McDonald's travel-hedging business (Just Get Out of Town, $6.4M trailing-12-month revenue, ~30% profit margin) had been running a single piece of paid creative on Meta at $100k/month with a spend ceiling: pushing to $150k in one month generated only 10% additional book sales. Alex Hormozi used this as a canonical example of a demand-constrained, creative-limited business, where the ceiling is not budget or market size but creative quality, and prescribed the UGC loop and Kaleidoscope method as the primary unlocks.

_from building_a_12_000_000_business_for_a_stranger_in_25_minutes_MH-IMJxbUY4.txt_

nodes.label: Alex Hormozi cited Old Spice's 'Man on a Horse' campaign as evidence that for ma…
nodes.description:
**Example:** Alex Hormozi cited Old Spice's 'Man on a Horse' campaign as evidence that for mass-market consumer products, one sufficiently resonant ad creative can move a brand from a small player to market leader. Old Spice had a minor share of men's body wash before the campaign; after it, they captured the majority of the category. Hormozi used this to argue that the theoretical ceiling on creative-driven scale is not a hard market cap but rather the quality of the creative.

_from building_a_12_000_000_business_for_a_stranger_in_25_minutes_MH-IMJxbUY4.txt_

nodes.label: Alex Hormozi described his experience running the School Games campaign at Acqui…
nodes.description:
**Example:** Alex Hormozi described his experience running the School Games campaign at Acquisition.com, where a single version of ad copy ran continuously for six months without creative fatigue, and a second portfolio company spending $200k+ per day had sustained only three winning hooks over five years. He used these cases to support the principle that winning copy should be left unchanged while only visual variants are refreshed.

_from building_a_12_000_000_business_for_a_stranger_in_25_minutes_MH-IMJxbUY4.txt_

nodes.label: Alex Hormozi illustrated the Kaleidoscope method with Joel McDonald's single exi…
nodes.description:
**Example:** Alex Hormozi illustrated the Kaleidoscope method with Joel McDonald's single existing top-converting ad image. He enumerated specific variation types: black-and-white filter, sepia filter, AI-animated 3-second video from the still, cartoonized version, Ghibli-style version, and trending meme treatments — demonstrating that one winning image could generate 20-30 distinct creatives without rebuilding the underlying offer or copy.

_from building_a_12_000_000_business_for_a_stranger_in_25_minutes_MH-IMJxbUY4.txt_

nodes.label: Alex Hormozi constructed a rough back-of-napkin lead flow for Joel McDonald's bu…
nodes.description:
**Example:** Alex Hormozi constructed a rough back-of-napkin lead flow for Joel McDonald's business: approximately 250 book sales per day, 700 mini-membership sign-ups per month (~23/day), and 1,000-1,500 new Facebook group members per month (~30/day). Assuming 10 of the 30 Facebook members provide a phone number (collectible if made mandatory with a free travel assessment as incentive), the total lead flow is roughly 300 prospects per day requiring sales outreach, which Hormozi used to derive the recommendation of 6 reps with a parallel dialer.

_from building_a_12_000_000_business_for_a_stranger_in_25_minutes_MH-IMJxbUY4.txt_

nodes.label: Alex Hormozi demonstrated the damaging admissions technique by scripting an exam…
nodes.description:
**Example:** Alex Hormozi demonstrated the damaging admissions technique by scripting an example for Joel McDonald's travel offer: 'Before I tell you the good, let me tell you the bad. If you want to go to Italy in June specifically, this won't work for you. If you want top-shelf places on your exact timeline, it won't work. But if you can take two weeks in mid-September versus June, then this is exactly right.' The technique allows skeptical prospects who can accept the constraints to self-qualify, while filtering out those who cannot, so that the remaining audience is genuinely qualified and believes the subsequent benefits.

_from building_a_12_000_000_business_for_a_stranger_in_25_minutes_MH-IMJxbUY4.txt_

nodes.label: Alex Hormozi reviewed Optimum Works' Google Ads account live during the session …
nodes.description:
**Example:** Alex Hormozi reviewed Optimum Works' Google Ads account live during the session and found that the agency-reported LTV-to-CAC ratio of 0.41:1 was flatly incompatible with the fact that the business was profitable. He reasoned that if 80% of sales were attributed to Google and each Google conversion was losing money on the reported ratio, the business should be losing money overall — but it was not. His proposed explanation: the agency had no idea what they were doing, and Optimum Works was actually receiving a large volume of referral and direct traffic from past buyers that was being incorrectly attributed to paid campaigns, making the ad spend appear both more costly and more impactful than it actually was.

_from building_a_1_000_000_business_for_a_stranger_in_26_minutes_HGZOxBfnF-E.txt_

nodes.label: At the one-year follow-up (March 2026), Luis Loira reported that once Optimum Wo…
nodes.description:
**Example:** At the one-year follow-up (March 2026), Luis Loira reported that once Optimum Works fixed attribution, they discovered specific campaigns that were breaking even or unprofitable. They reallocated the budget from those campaigns to the profitable winners. This single change — budget reallocation enabled only by clean attribution data — was described by Luis as one of the two highest-impact changes made over the year, alongside the custom-order sales process improvement.

_from building_a_1_000_000_business_for_a_stranger_in_26_minutes_HGZOxBfnF-E.txt_

nodes.label: During the session, Alex Hormozi reviewed the customer segmentation data for Opt…
nodes.description:
**Example:** During the session, Alex Hormozi reviewed the customer segmentation data for Optimum Works and noted that the average order value for DIY buyers ($873) was very close to the average for contractors and designers — not substantially different. He then argued that this equivalence eliminated the primary reason to pursue the contractor/designer segment (higher ticket), while the DIY segment offered a unique advantage: emotional investment in the product. A DIY buyer who has already self-selected on aesthetics is far more convertible to a custom order than a contractor comparing multiple fabricators on a spec sheet.

_from building_a_1_000_000_business_for_a_stranger_in_26_minutes_HGZOxBfnF-E.txt_

nodes.label: Alex Hormozi walked through the full custom-order sales funnel live during the s…
nodes.description:
**Example:** Alex Hormozi walked through the full custom-order sales funnel live during the session: the buyer clicks a custom-order CTA on any product listing page, fills out a short form, books a call via an embedded calendar, watches a 5-7 minute VSL explaining how to choose railings and covering price ranges, then receives BANT-focused SMS messages (budget, authority, need, timing) before the call. On the call, the rep closes with a credit-card-or-financing A/B close and a $200 on-call discount that was pre-disclosed in the nurture sequence. Hormozi estimated this process would yield 50-60% close rates on custom orders.

_from building_a_1_000_000_business_for_a_stranger_in_26_minutes_HGZOxBfnF-E.txt_

nodes.label: One year after Hormozi's session with Optimum Works, Luis Loira reported that cu…
nodes.description:
**Example:** One year after Hormozi's session with Optimum Works, Luis Loira reported that custom orders had grown from 30% to 50% of total business. He tripled the number of custom-order leads submitted by expanding the custom CTA across all product pages and improving the custom-order landing page. Despite raising prices, the custom-order close rate settled at 20% — lower than Hormozi's 50-60% projection but still sufficient to produce 44% revenue growth and 40% profit growth in 12 months.

_from building_a_1_000_000_business_for_a_stranger_in_26_minutes_HGZOxBfnF-E.txt_

nodes.label: Corey's ProShine HVAC cleaning business had already implemented a 23% price incr…
nodes.description:
**Example:** Corey's ProShine HVAC cleaning business had already implemented a 23% price increase following advice from an earlier Acquisition.com workshop. The result was counterintuitive: close rate went up and total revenue increased. Hormozi used this as a live illustration of the mechanism that higher prices raise buyer conviction in the seller's ability to deliver — demonstrating the virtuous cycle of pricing in a real, tracked business outcome.

_from building_a_2_500_000_business_for_a_stranger_in_36_minutes_OQf2Ba-Lp_4.txt_

nodes.label: Hormozi reviewed ProShine's existing Google Ads landing page on camera. The page…
nodes.description:
**Example:** Hormozi reviewed ProShine's existing Google Ads landing page on camera. The page directed all ad traffic to the business homepage, where the booking form was buried below the fold and the top navigation contained multiple competing links. He showed that a visitor clicking the ad first saw a large header bar, logo, and navigation menu before any offer — and that on mobile, the actual conversion action was not visible without scrolling. He recommended a dedicated, standalone landing page with the offer as the first visible element, no navigation, and a single CTA — and projected this alone could double or more the lead conversion rate.

_from building_a_2_500_000_business_for_a_stranger_in_36_minutes_OQf2Ba-Lp_4.txt_

nodes.label: Hormozi walked through ProShine's existing Facebook ad on camera. When he zoomed…
nodes.description:
**Example:** Hormozi walked through ProShine's existing Facebook ad on camera. When he zoomed out to approximate phone-screen display size, the 18-point inspection offer became unreadable, the checkmark callouts disappeared, and the only legible elements were a photo of Corey and his wife and the largest text block. He noted this was likely the highest-converting element for that reason. He recommended rebuilding the ad with the free 18-point inspection as the dominant typographic element at full readable size, running 40+ color/background variations, and eliminating logo-heavy design for direct response placements.

_from building_a_2_500_000_business_for_a_stranger_in_36_minutes_OQf2Ba-Lp_4.txt_

nodes.label: Corey's ProShine had one affiliate partner sending approximately $30,000 per mon…
nodes.description:
**Example:** Corey's ProShine had one affiliate partner sending approximately $30,000 per month in referral revenue. Hormozi noted this partner model worked because ProShine deliberately avoided competing in high-ticket HVAC replacement jobs, creating a non-threatening complementary relationship. Hormozi then pointed out that the reciprocal referral model could not scale to 20 partners because ProShine could not generate enough inbound volume to reciprocate meaningfully to all of them — proposing the lead-magnet upsell structure as a cash-incentive replacement that removes the reciprocity constraint entirely.

_from building_a_2_500_000_business_for_a_stranger_in_36_minutes_OQf2Ba-Lp_4.txt_

nodes.label: Hormozi drew the gym-industry seasonal campaign parallel to illustrate the pre/d…
nodes.description:
**Example:** Hormozi drew the gym-industry seasonal campaign parallel to illustrate the pre/during/post seasonal framing concept. In the gym world, two seasonal demand spikes exist: New Year's fitness resolutions and summer beach body preparation. From those two spikes, a gym can generate six campaign slots — pre-New Year, New Year hit, resolution check-in (February), pre-summer, summer in-season, and missed-resolution re-entry — running year-round coverage from just two seasonal pain points. He then mapped this framework to ProShine's allergy season (spring pollen) and heating season (mildew smell from heating elements), showing how the same six-slot model applies.

_from building_a_2_500_000_business_for_a_stranger_in_36_minutes_OQf2Ba-Lp_4.txt_

nodes.label: Hormozi described a reactivation email framing for ProShine: instead of the exis…
nodes.plugin: Theme-Driven Email Reactivation with Split Testing
nodes.description:
**Example:** Hormozi described a reactivation email framing for ProShine: instead of the existing 'we recommend a yearly checkup' tone, he proposed subject lines like 'I owe you money' or 'we made a mistake on your account' with body copy framing the free dryer vent inspection as a benefit the customer was promised at signup but never received. He suggested split-testing this against the existing neutral-tone email in back-to-back weeks and measuring open rates and booking rates, because the cost of the test is zero beyond writing time.

_from building_a_2_500_000_business_for_a_stranger_in_36_minutes_OQf2Ba-Lp_4.txt_
