nodes.label: Planet Fitness entered a crowded gym market at $10/month by surveying existing h…
nodes.description:
**Example:** Planet Fitness entered a crowded gym market at $10/month by surveying existing health club members ($59/month with pools, basketball courts, racket courts, etc.) and discovering that the vast majority only used cardio equipment and a small amount of weight equipment — approximately 10-15% of the facility. Planet Fitness stripped out everything else, offered only those two amenities, and charged drastically less. The key retention insight: when customers pay for five services but use only one, they perceive 20% value utilization and feel justified in canceling; when the same price covers only that one service, they feel 100% utilized and stay. This illustrates that adding features to a recurring product increases perceived underutilization and therefore churn.

_from how_to_get_your_customers_to_stay_forever_-j8_YCWZ05Q.txt_

nodes.label: A School community operator applied the content-deletion principle and deleted e…
nodes.description:
**Example:** A School community operator applied the content-deletion principle and deleted existing content from their platform. Their monthly churn dropped from 30% to 5%, a ~6x increase in LTV. Hormozi cites this as direct evidence that content volume in membership businesses drives felt underutilization, which is the primary churn mechanism outside of price.

_from how_to_get_your_customers_to_stay_forever_-j8_YCWZ05Q.txt_

nodes.label: Alex Hormozi describes how he managed new-member belonging at his gym businesses…
nodes.description:
**Example:** Alex Hormozi describes how he managed new-member belonging at his gym businesses by identifying true regulars and personally introducing new members to them by name, stating each person's relevant skill or interest to seed rapport. He describes the experience as preventing new members from feeling like they walked in on someone else's party. This illustrates the one-real-friend retention mechanism applied in a physical community context.

_from how_to_get_your_customers_to_stay_forever_-j8_YCWZ05Q.txt_

nodes.label: School (the platform) placed the head of customer support physically adjacent to…
nodes.description:
**Example:** School (the platform) placed the head of customer support physically adjacent to Sam Ovens (CEO) in the office so that product development received a tight feedback loop from cancellation reasons and customer complaints. Hormozi cites this structural arrangement as a key reason School became a strong platform — problems surfaced quickly and were built into the roadmap rather than ignored.

_from how_to_get_your_customers_to_stay_forever_-j8_YCWZ05Q.txt_

nodes.label: Hormozi frames the original questioner's situation as self-defeating: a founder …
nodes.description:
**Example:** Hormozi frames the original questioner's situation as self-defeating: a founder struggling to get clients for a high-ticket lead generation offer has failed to generate their own leads, which is the service they are selling. He uses this as an illustration of how the absence of proof is compounded when the service category is marketing — the inability to self-market is not neutral, it is active negative evidence in the prospect's mind.

_from how_to_get_your_first_clients_with_zero_proof_QgvX_5km_Yo.txt_

nodes.label: Hormozi describes the specific offer structure for the lead-with-free strategy: …
nodes.description:
**Example:** Hormozi describes the specific offer structure for the lead-with-free strategy: tell prospects you will work with them for free, doing five one-on-one calls at no charge. At the end of the fifth call, the founder offers to continue for free or convert to a paid arrangement at a stated price. This structure creates a defined evaluation window for both parties without requiring the prospect to make a financial commitment upfront.

_from how_to_get_your_first_clients_with_zero_proof_QgvX_5km_Yo.txt_

nodes.label: Alex Hormozi launched the Guinness World Record-breaking book as an e-commerce o…
nodes.description:
**Example:** Alex Hormozi launched the Guinness World Record-breaking book as an e-commerce operation, requiring him to find multiple third-party logistics providers across different US states capable of shipping millions of units within 72 hours. This illustrated that even a book launch operates under e-commerce constraints: fulfillment partner capacity and geographic logistics redundancy become the ceiling on delivery speed, not demand or marketing.

_from how_to_grow_any_business_faster_masterclass_qsXxckCbci0.txt_

nodes.label: Alex Hormozi describes Prestige Labs as his physical products e-commerce experie…
nodes.description:
**Example:** Alex Hormozi describes Prestige Labs as his physical products e-commerce experience, selling through both brick-and-mortar gym distribution and a direct-to-consumer online store with paid advertising. He used it to illustrate that e-commerce businesses inherently have dual distribution dependencies (brick-and-mortar partners and ad-based distribution) and that the growth ceiling is set by whichever distribution channel or supply chain element saturates first.

_from how_to_grow_any_business_faster_masterclass_qsXxckCbci0.txt_

nodes.label: Discussing the fitness coaching business as a service model, Alex Hormozi notes …
nodes.description:
**Example:** Discussing the fitness coaching business as a service model, Alex Hormozi notes it is an unusual example within service businesses because talent is easy to attract (many people would coach fitness for free) but demand and retention are hard because customers dislike working out. He contrasts this with the majority of done-for-you service businesses (roofing, accounting, legal, web development) where talent is hard to find but customer retention is strong because clients do not want to learn or do the work themselves.

_from how_to_grow_any_business_faster_masterclass_qsXxckCbci0.txt_

nodes.label: Alex Hormozi described his own progression in service businesses as evidence of …
nodes.description:
**Example:** Alex Hormozi described his own progression in service businesses as evidence of the model's characteristics: he scaled six brick-and-mortar gyms (B2C service), performed over 30 gym turnarounds across nearly two years (B2C service consulting), built an online gym consulting firm offering marketing and ad creation services to gym owners in English-speaking markets up to mid-$30M revenue (B2B service), and currently operates Acquisition.com's advisory practice, which is described as a nine-figure-plus white-collar B2B service business.

_from how_to_grow_any_business_faster_masterclass_qsXxckCbci0.txt_

nodes.label: Alex Hormozi described the Acquisition.com advisory practice as a high-end profe…
nodes.description:
**Example:** Alex Hormozi described the Acquisition.com advisory practice as a high-end professional service business modeled after management consulting. Associates begin as junior analysts and progress through a defined career path to senior associates and then directors over multiple years, in a deliberate apprenticeship model he compared to accounting, management consulting, and legal firms. This illustrated the core service business tenet that talent takes years to develop and requires defined career paths to be retained.

_from how_to_grow_any_business_faster_masterclass_qsXxckCbci0.txt_

nodes.label: Alex Hormozi described School.com, which he co-founded, as an example of a softw…
nodes.description:
**Example:** Alex Hormozi described School.com, which he co-founded, as an example of a software platform (SaaS) that has reached 20 million users. He used it to illustrate the tension in software product management between adding features (which customers request) and maintaining simplicity (which is required for good user experience); he noted that adding features almost always adds complexity, which is the antithesis of the elegant user experience that drives retention.

_from how_to_grow_any_business_faster_masterclass_qsXxckCbci0.txt_

nodes.label: Alex Hormozi cited the Dropbox founder's practice of paying Craigslist participa…
nodes.description:
**Example:** Alex Hormozi cited the Dropbox founder's practice of paying Craigslist participants to come in and attempt to upload a file while being observed. In the first round, five out of five users failed to upload a file because they could not figure out the interface. The team then iterated on the UI for weeks and repeated the process until users successfully completed the core action. This illustrated that product-market fit in SaaS requires obsessive user experience iteration, not marketing, before any growth investment is worthwhile.

_from how_to_grow_any_business_faster_masterclass_qsXxckCbci0.txt_

nodes.label: Alex Hormozi cited ChatGPT reaching one million users in one week as an example …
nodes.description:
**Example:** Alex Hormozi cited ChatGPT reaching one million users in one week as an example of virality enabling rapid SaaS growth without proportional paid acquisition spend. He contrasted this with Facebook's approach: Facebook spent significant money to acquire initial customers but knew its viral coefficient would mean each paid acquisition generated two or more additional users organically, compounding down the effective blended CAC.

_from how_to_grow_any_business_faster_masterclass_qsXxckCbci0.txt_

nodes.label: Alex Hormozi used Warren Buffett and Berkshire Hathaway as the canonical illustr…
nodes.description:
**Example:** Alex Hormozi used Warren Buffett and Berkshire Hathaway as the canonical illustration of real-world proof in education. He argued that if someone took every piece of investment knowledge Warren Buffett has ever shared publicly and turned it into a course on long-term investing, almost nobody would buy it. The missing element is Berkshire Hathaway: $89 billion in profit, starting from age seven, over nearly 100 years. Without that proof, the identical educational content would be unmarketable at premium prices.

_from how_to_grow_any_business_faster_masterclass_qsXxckCbci0.txt_

nodes.label: Alex Hormozi described the ACQAI and book bundle launch as a hybrid education-pl…
nodes.description:
**Example:** Alex Hormozi described the ACQAI and book bundle launch as a hybrid education-plus-e-commerce event that generated from zero to $100 million in approximately 60 hours. He attributed the velocity to three factors: a large audience with positive prior experience from his free content and previous books, a strong promotional skill set, and a high-quality product that built trust through each preceding book in the series. He used this to illustrate how combined business model shapes can create unusual revenue spikes not possible with any single model.

_from how_to_grow_any_business_faster_masterclass_qsXxckCbci0.txt_

nodes.label: Alex Hormozi described his own hiring learning curve as illustrative of the patt…
nodes.description:
**Example:** Alex Hormozi described his own hiring learning curve as illustrative of the pattern-matching process: in his first business he had no idea what a strong salesperson looked like until he hired one and was able to observe the template. Once he could recognize the pattern, he could duplicate it. Then he did not know what a sales manager looked like, so he cycled through more hires until one revealed the pattern. He noted this process repeats at every new role and every new seniority level — the first time you hire a CFO, you don't know what a good CFO looks like; once you find one, you do. He argued that experienced operators can rebuild businesses faster precisely because they have accumulated more of these mental templates across roles and levels.

_from how_to_hire_the_right_leadership_team_as_you_scale_n7CYRXrdebU.txt_

nodes.label: The skincare business owner described her company's prior recruiting problem: wh…
nodes.description:
**Example:** The skincare business owner described her company's prior recruiting problem: when scaling the phone sales team, she would increase ad spend, generate more leads than the team could call, watch margins drop, and get stuck. She solved that by building a dedicated sales recruitment team. She is now facing an identical structural constraint at the leadership level — the absence of C-suite roles is pulling her and her COO Kyle out of strategic work into day-to-day fires, preventing growth toward the $25M/month target. Hormozi confirmed this pattern: she has built the operational base layer but is missing the top leadership layer.

_from how_to_hire_the_right_leadership_team_as_you_scale_n7CYRXrdebU.txt_

nodes.label: Alex Hormozi gave a concrete example of how he and Layla handle major hiring con…
nodes.description:
**Example:** Alex Hormozi gave a concrete example of how he and Layla handle major hiring constraints at Acquisition.com: they pull themselves entirely out of other business activities and run a dedicated six-week sprint focused exclusively on interviews. He noted that during that sprint he would not be meeting with directors or managers, only C-suite-level candidates — because at that level his personal involvement in the process is the appropriate use of founder time.

_from how_to_hire_the_right_leadership_team_as_you_scale_n7CYRXrdebU.txt_

nodes.label: Hormozi gave a legal example of using existing trusted experts to vet unfamiliar…
nodes.description:
**Example:** Hormozi gave a legal example of using existing trusted experts to vet unfamiliar hires: when needing to hire in-house counsel, he called attorneys he already pays and asked them to interview the candidate on the technical and legal competency side. This allowed him to evaluate only the cultural and organizational fit elements himself, relying on domain experts he trusts for the skills assessment he could not independently conduct.

_from how_to_hire_the_right_leadership_team_as_you_scale_n7CYRXrdebU.txt_

nodes.label: Alex Hormozi encountered a contact who bragged that he had cut his content effor…
nodes.description:
**Example:** Alex Hormozi encountered a contact who bragged that he had cut his content effort down to two hours per week, presenting it as a virtue of efficiency and claiming to like bragging about it. Hormozi responded simply: 'Yeah, it shows.' The contact was trying to appear cool by not trying hard, but the visible output was indistinguishable from losing.

_from how_to_make_progress_faster_than_everyone_yb2cLMMuMdQ.txt_

nodes.label: Alex Hormozi describes the moment he deliberately began documenting his journey:…
nodes.description:
**Example:** Alex Hormozi describes the moment he deliberately began documenting his journey: the day he had $1,000 left in his bank account after losing everything. At that moment he decided to document intentionally, treating it as the first frame of his comeback story. He describes Kanye West as a parallel example — someone who documented obsessively in the early days because he believed so hardcore he would win.

_from how_to_make_progress_faster_than_everyone_yb2cLMMuMdQ.txt_

nodes.label: Alex Hormozi shows publicly the first ad he ever made, his first professional ad…
nodes.description:
**Example:** Alex Hormozi shows publicly the first ad he ever made, his first professional ad, his first content piece, his first YouTube video, and his first Instagram post. All are described as genuinely bad by his own assessment — the first content piece has no strong hook, no strong meet, no strong payoff. Ninety days after his first ad, he lost everything for the second time and created his first podcast as a way to document lessons for his own future reference.

_from how_to_make_progress_faster_than_everyone_yb2cLMMuMdQ.txt_

nodes.label: Alex Hormozi uses a list of activities that can each be made to sound ridiculous…
nodes.description:
**Example:** Alex Hormozi uses a list of activities that can each be made to sound ridiculous through framing: competitive bodybuilding (oiling up and posing in tiny trunks), competitive chess (staring at wooden pieces in silence), making YouTube videos (talking to a camera like an idiot), and writing a book (locking yourself away for months to type at a keyboard no one will read). The point: any committed activity is describable in trivializing terms, so the cringe label reflects the framer's lens, not the activity's worth.

_from how_to_make_progress_faster_than_everyone_yb2cLMMuMdQ.txt_

nodes.label: Alex Hormozi illustrates the operational definition of learning with a door-gree…
nodes.description:
**Example:** Alex Hormozi illustrates the operational definition of learning with a door-greeting exercise: someone is taught to say 'welcome to Starbucks' instead of 'hi, this is Alex' when the door is knocked. The triggering condition (knock-knock) stays constant. If they revert to the old greeting on the next knock, no learning occurred. If they say 'welcome to Starbucks,' learning occurred. Hormozi uses this to show that intelligence can be measured as the number of knock-knock events required before the response consistently changes.

_from how_to_outlearn_everyone_q9qBqnhdWKw.txt_

nodes.label: Alex Hormozi describes his experience at Vanderbilt University (ranked top 5-7 i…
nodes.description:
**Example:** Alex Hormozi describes his experience at Vanderbilt University (ranked top 5-7 in the US at the time) where he felt his classmates had superior intellectual capacity. His solution was to study from 9 AM to 9 PM every day, leaving the library only for class, the cafeteria, and the gym. He concluded that although peers might change their behavior in 3 iterations, by doing 10 iterations in the same day he changed his behavior faster on a calendar basis than they did with fewer iterations spread over weeks.

_from how_to_outlearn_everyone_q9qBqnhdWKw.txt_

nodes.label: Alex Hormozi uses a tennis grip lesson as an example of the ignore-the-black-box…
nodes.description:
**Example:** Alex Hormozi uses a tennis grip lesson as an example of the ignore-the-black-box principle. He asks: when a tennis pro corrects your grip, do they say 'let's discover why you grip incorrectly and explore what teachers failed to teach you'? No. They correct the grip. Hormozi uses this to argue that seeking psychological explanations before correcting behavior delays learning without adding value.

_from how_to_outlearn_everyone_q9qBqnhdWKw.txt_

nodes.label: Alex Hormozi illustrates observational learning with a social influence scenario…
nodes.description:
**Example:** Alex Hormozi illustrates observational learning with a social influence scenario: by watching a high-influence person interact, he notes that the influential person enters the room, smiles, shakes hands, stands with contracted traps and mid-back (upright posture), and nods when the other person speaks while occasionally interjecting. Rather than asking why this creates compliance, Hormozi models the physical behaviors and tests whether they change outcomes. He uses this to demonstrate that breaking influence down into observable micro-behaviors is both actionable and replicable.

_from how_to_outlearn_everyone_q9qBqnhdWKw.txt_

nodes.label: Alex Hormozi describes his iterative improvement model using Instagram Reels as …
nodes.description:
**Example:** Alex Hormozi describes his iterative improvement model using Instagram Reels as a concrete domain. You create a large volume of reels. You identify your top 10% by views and likes. You observe what those reels did differently from the others. You extract one or two behavioral differences. You then produce another batch of many reels incorporating those differences. You identify the new top 10% and repeat. Each pass adds a coat of paint to your observational understanding until patterns that were invisible early on become apparent.

_from how_to_outlearn_everyone_q9qBqnhdWKw.txt_

nodes.label: Alex Hormozi references a conversation with Amjad (CEO/founder of Replit) about …
nodes.description:
**Example:** Alex Hormozi references a conversation with Amjad (CEO/founder of Replit) about AI training as an analogy for skill learning: AI must first be trained on labeled data (good/bad) from external sources, just as humans model top performers. Once AI can learn in the real world from first-party driving data, feedback loops accelerate dramatically. Hormozi uses this to justify the transition from modeling others to learning from your own high-volume attempts once sufficient data exists.

_from how_to_outlearn_everyone_q9qBqnhdWKw.txt_

nodes.label: Alex Hormozi shares a personal story about buying a Powerball lottery ticket aro…
nodes.plugin: Effort Compounds Relative to Starting Conditions
nodes.description:
**Example:** Alex Hormozi shares a personal story about buying a Powerball lottery ticket around 2020-2021 when the jackpot was approximately $1 billion. As the drawing happened, he experienced terror at the possibility of winning, because he believed that winning would permanently prevent him from proving that he could succeed through his own efforts. He did not win and describes feeling relieved, using this to illustrate that luck, by removing the challenge, also removes the opportunity to become who you are capable of becoming.

_from how_to_outlearn_everyone_q9qBqnhdWKw.txt_
nodes.parent_id: concept:Effort Compounds Relative to Starting Conditions
nodes.topic: Effort Compounds Relative to Starting Conditions

nodes.label: Alex Hormozi cites Michael Jordan as an example of the gap between performing a …
nodes.description:
**Example:** Alex Hormozi cites Michael Jordan as an example of the gap between performing a skill and teaching it. Jordan is widely considered the best basketball player of all time, but Hormozi asserts he was not a notably effective coach. The argument: Jordan's skill execution was automatic and largely non-conscious, so his verbal explanations of how he played were not accurate causal accounts; they were verbal responses conditioned by receiving positive social reactions when asked. Teaching is a separate skill from performing.

_from how_to_outlearn_everyone_q9qBqnhdWKw.txt_

nodes.label: A micro-development housing company doing $46M in revenue and targeting $500M as…
nodes.plugin: Conferences and Events as High-Leverage Channels
nodes.description:
**Example:** A micro-development housing company doing $46M in revenue and targeting $500M asked Alex Hormozi how to attract high-net-worth accredited investors without using their personal network. Hormozi outlined the four available channels (affiliate, paid ads, content, outbound), noted trade shows collapse into the affiliate bucket, then recommended conferences and events as the highest-leverage starting point because investor relationships are enterprise-grade and face-to-face trust builds fastest. He added the caveat that a founder with media-buying experience might reasonably start with paid ads instead.

_from how_to_raise_capital_without_using_your_personal_network_EjBgv-DGJ-M.txt_
nodes.parent_id: concept:Conferences and Events as High-Leverage Channels
nodes.topic: Conferences and Events as High-Leverage Channels

nodes.label: The dietitian consulting business featured in this session (K-Specific Wellness,…
nodes.description:
**Example:** The dietitian consulting business featured in this session (K-Specific Wellness, Pennsylvania) illustrates hidden cost blindness in action. The founder had achieved 35-50% year-over-year growth for three years, fixed all operational breakpoints over two years, and built a provider network generating ~400 referrals per month across 18 ancillary practitioners. Despite this strong trajectory, the founder was actively exploring franchising, licensing, a gym adjacency, and a dietitian training university simultaneously, spreading attention thin. Alex Hormozi pointed out that VC-funded competitors with substantial capital and talented teams had not been able to make the virtual-only model profitable, which the founder himself confirmed via two acquisition offers made to him by those same groups seeking his quality metrics. This made the case that the apparent advantage of the new model was an illusion: the costs were invisible because no one in the industry had yet paid them at scale.

_from how_to_say_no_to_the_wrong_opportunities_YJy7PL2apUo.txt_

nodes.label: Alex Hormozi used Panda Express as a concrete illustration that patient single-m…
nodes.description:
**Example:** Alex Hormozi used Panda Express as a concrete illustration that patient single-model scaling produces extraordinary wealth without model pivots. He described Mr. Panda (the founder) as a neighbor who built a 3.7 billion dollar top-line business at 27% net margin by selling chicken for 45 years one location at a time. The example was used to counter the founder's feeling that 10 years was too long to reach his revenue targets within the existing model: Hormozi framed the 10-year path to $40M as a genuinely life-changing outcome that the founder was discounting because it felt slow compared to flashy VC-funded competitors.

_from how_to_say_no_to_the_wrong_opportunities_YJy7PL2apUo.txt_

nodes.label: Hormozi illustrated the franchise economics problem using the founder's own numb…
nodes.description:
**Example:** Hormozi illustrated the franchise economics problem using the founder's own numbers. The dietitian practice generates ~$500K per location at ~15% net margin, yielding ~$75K profit per location for the direct owner. A licensing fee of 6-8% of top line would yield $30-40K per location per year for the licensor, with no capital at risk but also no operational control. Hormozi used this comparison to show that licensing is acceptable for the low-margin situation (taking half the profit off the top line without deploying capital) whereas franchising is economically inferior because the franchisor gives away full business ownership for essentially the same royalty stream.

_from how_to_say_no_to_the_wrong_opportunities_YJy7PL2apUo.txt_

nodes.label: Alex Hormozi tells the ham-and-garlic story to illustrate the ham-and-garlic fra…
nodes.description:
**Example:** Alex Hormozi tells the ham-and-garlic story to illustrate the ham-and-garlic framework: a boy begs his father for a dog, the father agrees on condition the boy takes full responsibility. The dog gets ticks while the father is away. The grandmother tells the boy to feed the dog garlic to sweat out the ticks. The dog refuses to eat raw garlic. The grandmother tells him to wrap the garlic in ham. The dog eats it, the ticks clear, the day is saved. The moral: give people what they want (ham) in order to give them what they need (garlic). Applied to the tutoring business: the short 3-week program is the ham; the year-long continuity engagement is the garlic.

_from how_to_scale_a_tutoring_business_from_250k_to_1m_U8Noy9ly7A4.txt_

nodes.label: Alex Hormozi gives the gym industry as a parallel example: no customer has ever …
nodes.description:
**Example:** Alex Hormozi gives the gym industry as a parallel example: no customer has ever walked into a gym and said they want a lifestyle. They buy a 6-week challenge, a 21-day detox, or a 28-day fix. After enrolling, the gym has a window to educate the customer on what really matters. The gym then upgrades them from the short program to a long-term membership once momentum is established (e.g., after losing 20 of 50 desired pounds, the customer is invested and ready to commit to a full solution).

_from how_to_scale_a_tutoring_business_from_250k_to_1m_U8Noy9ly7A4.txt_

nodes.label: The tutoring business owner reports that after changing Facebook ad targeting fr…
nodes.description:
**Example:** The tutoring business owner reports that after changing Facebook ad targeting from the 35+ age bracket (reaching parents) to a minimum of 25 (the new platform limit), student traffic flooded in instead of parent traffic. Despite the cost per lead dropping by 75%, none of the leads converted because students are not the economic decision-maker for tutoring purchases; parents are. This illustrates that lower cost-per-lead is meaningless when the lead pool is the wrong avatar.

_from how_to_scale_a_tutoring_business_from_250k_to_1m_U8Noy9ly7A4.txt_

nodes.label: Alex Hormozi cited three businesses where he built distribution layers using the…
nodes.description:
**Example:** Alex Hormozi cited three businesses where he built distribution layers using the two-pronged launch-plus-retention strategy: Prestige Labs (supplement company), Allen (software company), and School (community platform). Each required an initial launch mechanism to give new distributors an immediate win, followed by an ongoing distributor customer journey to sustain usage and reduce churn.

_from how_to_scale_a_white_label_agency_past_1_5m_0coMtm_i1UA.txt_

nodes.label: The white-label PR agency founder described a prior unlimited-articles plan at $…
nodes.description:
**Example:** The white-label PR agency founder described a prior unlimited-articles plan at $2,500/month that generated higher revenue than the current $1,000/month plan. However, it created extreme usage variance — one agency published 900 articles per month while another published only 10. The wide variance made unit economics unpredictable and made it impossible to profit from the low-usage majority while serving the high-usage outliers.

_from how_to_scale_a_white_label_agency_past_1_5m_0coMtm_i1UA.txt_

nodes.label: The white-label PR agency owner reported being stuck at $1.5M for five consecuti…
nodes.description:
**Example:** The white-label PR agency owner reported being stuck at $1.5M for five consecutive years despite using all available advertising channels and spending significant money on ads with poor returns. Hormozi identified within the conversation that the root cause was not lead generation failure but rather high churn among distributor agencies who white-labeled the service — the acquisition bucket was refilling while the retention bucket emptied at a matching rate.

_from how_to_scale_a_white_label_agency_past_1_5m_0coMtm_i1UA.txt_

nodes.label: Alex Hormozi illustrates behavioral learning with a phone-answer training scenar…
nodes.description:
**Example:** Alex Hormozi illustrates behavioral learning with a phone-answer training scenario. A trainee is taught to answer the phone with greeting Z instead of their habitual X. On the next call, if they revert to X, no learning has occurred. If they say Z, learning has occurred. The condition (phone rings) is held constant; the only variable is the response. This shows that learning is strictly defined by observable behavior change, not self-reported understanding.

_from how_to_see_reality_more_clearly_than_99_of_people_8YJEyMYYwnE.txt_

nodes.label: Alex Hormozi uses patience as a worked example of the observable-definition meth…
nodes.description:
**Example:** Alex Hormozi uses patience as a worked example of the observable-definition method. Abstract instruction (be patient) gives a child no actionable target. Observable translation: find something else to do in the meantime. Hormozi notes that this is precisely what adults do with long-horizon investments like S&P 500 accounts, they occupy themselves with other activities rather than watching the account. The observable definition collapses a vague virtue into a concrete, repeatable action.

_from how_to_see_reality_more_clearly_than_99_of_people_8YJEyMYYwnE.txt_

nodes.label: Alex Hormozi describes resolving a leadership conflict by translating the abstra…
nodes.description:
**Example:** Alex Hormozi describes resolving a leadership conflict by translating the abstract complaint he's acting like a dick into two to three specific observable behaviors: interrupting during meetings and telling people how to do their jobs. He told the employee he did not care about the label, only about reducing the behaviors that caused others to apply it. He also clarified that failed execution after the employee's suggestions was the manager's accountability problem, not the employee's. After eliminating those specific behaviors, the employee's reputation reversed fully and the formal complaints stopped.

_from how_to_see_reality_more_clearly_than_99_of_people_8YJEyMYYwnE.txt_

nodes.label: Alex Hormozi describes discovering that his personal anger behavior toward his w…
nodes.description:
**Example:** Alex Hormozi describes discovering that his personal anger behavior toward his wife Layla Hormozi was being maintained by a reinforcement loop he did not consciously recognize. When Layla cried during conflicts, Hormozi would attempt comfort; if comfort failed, he would become angry. Layla's fear response caused her to stop crying. This outcome (crying stops) reinforced the anger behavior. Hormozi only identified this in retrospect and noted that he had long misattributed the behavior to a trigger (her crying) rather than to its reinforcer (her silence afterward). Recognizing the consequence-based driver was the prerequisite for working to change it.

_from how_to_see_reality_more_clearly_than_99_of_people_8YJEyMYYwnE.txt_

nodes.label: Alex Hormozi illustrates the lazy label problem with a scenario involving a pers…
nodes.description:
**Example:** Alex Hormozi illustrates the lazy label problem with a scenario involving a person named John. A manager thinks John is lazy. Hormozi walks through the analysis: what observable events caused that assessment? The answer: John responds slowly and arrived ill-prepared to one meeting. Translated into behavioral instructions, the correction becomes give responses in under five minutes and send meeting notes ahead of time. The abstract label lazy disappears after those specific behaviors change, demonstrating that abstract trait labels routinely over-summarize a small number of specific correctable behaviors.

_from how_to_see_reality_more_clearly_than_99_of_people_8YJEyMYYwnE.txt_

nodes.label: Alex Hormozi uses the wedding photographer niche as an illustrative case. He not…
nodes.description:
**Example:** Alex Hormozi uses the wedding photographer niche as an illustrative case. He notes that while generating leads in this space is easy via Google Ads, the market is commoditized because nearly everyone with a camera labels themselves a photographer. The practical consequence is that raw lead quality is low: prospects are shopping around rather than committed to a premium purchase. This structural reality, Hormozi argues, is why any agency selling services at $2K+ in this space must add qualification friction to the front of the funnel before investing significant sales effort on each lead.

_from how_to_sell_a_2k_service_in_a_saturated_market_trAAFADIAZw.txt_

nodes.label: A restaurant franchise owner with four corporate locations doing $9M in revenue …
nodes.description:
**Example:** A restaurant franchise owner with four corporate locations doing $9M in revenue and $1.2M in profit, plus one open franchise unit and two more signed, approached Alex Hormozi for advice on selling more franchises. He believed franchises could not be actively sold because the purchase required a lifestyle change, and therefore buyers had to self-select. Hormozi rejected the passive framing and reoriented the conversation: the difficulty selling franchises was not a sales methodology problem but a unit economics problem. The franchisee offer was not compelling enough, and improving per-unit profitability — not marketing or sales tactics — was the required first step.

_from how_to_sell_more_franchises_without_selling_them_0ZwRf4Dy_MM.txt_

nodes.label: The business owner in the transcript grew a residential plumbing and HVAC compan…
nodes.description:
**Example:** The business owner in the transcript grew a residential plumbing and HVAC company from $4M to $8M to $11M and was pacing $15M by hiring two leaders from outside the industry. Despite this top-line growth, net profit margin stayed flat at roughly 14-16%, and the absolute dollar gain was real but came with operational chaos, frequent errors, and no improvement in the percentage of revenue kept as profit. Hormozi used this as a live example of a business that had optimized for revenue at the expense of margin, and reframed the goal: stay at $15M revenue, fix the sales motion and pricing, and target 30% net — which would approximately double the owner's annual take-home without any additional revenue growth.

_from how_to_triple_profit_without_growing_revenue_9Xmcfgf1tsc.txt_

nodes.label: The business owner disclosed that the two executives driving top-line growth wer…
nodes.description:
**Example:** The business owner disclosed that the two executives driving top-line growth were compensated on net profit but behaved as top-line revenue maximizers. When Hormozi asked what they were compensated on and heard net, he noted that the behavior — single-mindedly chasing revenue volume — was inconsistent with the stated incentive. The owner's explanation was that the executives came from large corporate environments where the cultural orientation was always toward bigger top-line numbers. This illustrated the gap between stated compensation structure and actual behavioral incentive when cultural norms override formal incentive design.

_from how_to_triple_profit_without_growing_revenue_9Xmcfgf1tsc.txt_

nodes.label: During Acquisition.com's book launch (prior to mainstream discussion of AI agent…
nodes.description:
**Example:** During Acquisition.com's book launch (prior to mainstream discussion of AI agents), the team deployed five AI agents to handle support traffic. The agents resolved approximately 90% of roughly 120,000 support tickets without human involvement. Most queries were simple fulfillment questions such as where to access free accompanying materials. The exercise demonstrated that predictable, high-volume, low-complexity support can be fully managed by AI given adequate training on product specifics.

_from how_to_use_ai_in_your_business_in_2026_fr78adfAnuA.txt_

nodes.label: Alex Hormozi illustrates the AI-as-tool analogy by noting that almost every busi…
nodes.description:
**Example:** Alex Hormozi illustrates the AI-as-tool analogy by noting that almost every business uses the internet but is not described as an internet business. A company using a webpage is not a tech company. The early businesses that established an internet presence captured disproportionate returns when having a webpage was still differentiating. Now the same dynamic is beginning with AI: early movers will capture outsized margin before AI adoption becomes as universal and unremarkable as having a website.

_from how_to_use_ai_in_your_business_in_2026_fr78adfAnuA.txt_

nodes.label: Alex Hormozi gives the example of content ideation automation: a bot checks the …
nodes.description:
**Example:** Alex Hormozi gives the example of content ideation automation: a bot checks the owner's calendar (step 1), transcribes all recorded calls taken that week (step 2), and then surfaces the five most interesting situations or decisions from that week's data (step 3). The output is a set of true, narrative-ready business moments that can be packaged as content without fabrication. This workflow illustrates both the decomposition of intuitive knowledge into observable steps and the value of calendar- and call-data as reality-sourced content inputs.

_from how_to_use_ai_in_your_business_in_2026_fr78adfAnuA.txt_

nodes.label: Alex Hormozi describes an automated ad pipeline where a community-owned school c…
nodes.description:
**Example:** Alex Hormozi describes an automated ad pipeline where a community-owned school captures member wins in a single tab; any new win entry automatically feeds into six high-converting visual templates and launches as a paid ad targeting the Vantage ($1M+ revenue) community. This self-executing loop converts user-generated proof directly into live ad creative with no human editorial step, illustrating how structured proof data combined with templated creative produces a compounding content and acquisition engine.

_from how_to_use_ai_in_your_business_in_2026_fr78adfAnuA.txt_

nodes.label: Alex Hormozi uses the analogy of transplanting a top salesperson from his compan…
nodes.description:
**Example:** Alex Hormozi uses the analogy of transplanting a top salesperson from his company into a client's business: on the first attempt the rep would perform poorly because they lack context about the new business, its customers, its offer, and its objections. Transplanting an AI sales agent is the same: without equivalent onboarding and contextual training, the AI will underperform. This example grounds the claim that AI implementation maturity requires the same investment of context as training a human.

_from how_to_use_ai_in_your_business_in_2026_fr78adfAnuA.txt_

nodes.label: Alex Hormozi describes how his general counsel can now run legal responses (firs…
nodes.description:
**Example:** Alex Hormozi describes how his general counsel can now run legal responses (first response, second response, cease-and-desist letters, deal review) through specialized AI agents rather than requiring a team of 100 paralegals. This allows one senior lawyer to manage the full scope of daily legal activity that would previously have required large support staff, illustrating the headcount leverage available through task-level AI deployment in professional functions.

_from how_to_use_ai_in_your_business_in_2026_fr78adfAnuA.txt_

nodes.label: Alex Hormozi describes a friend who is a successful entrepreneur and has launche…
nodes.description:
**Example:** Alex Hormozi describes a friend who is a successful entrepreneur and has launched an internal division whose sole mission is to put his much larger legacy business out of business. The friend allocates 20% of his time to this effort. This illustrates the claim that the most adaptive business operators are actively attempting to automate themselves rather than waiting for a competitor to do it.

_from how_to_win_with_ai_in_2026_9q5ojtkqsBs.txt_

nodes.label: Hormozi cites Anthropic as an example of AI-enabled organizational leverage: Ant…
nodes.description:
**Example:** Hormozi cites Anthropic as an example of AI-enabled organizational leverage: Anthropic reportedly runs its entire marketing function with one person. Hormozi acknowledges that Anthropic also benefits from significant earned media and PR, but his point is that one person with well-trained AI agents can produce the output previously requiring a full department, illustrating the BYOS / BYOA model.

_from how_to_win_with_ai_in_2026_9q5ojtkqsBs.txt_

nodes.label: Hormozi gives a concrete AI training illustration: if you tell an AI to write em…
nodes.description:
**Example:** Hormozi gives a concrete AI training illustration: if you tell an AI to write email copy without additional context, it produces generic internet-sounding output because it was trained on the internet as a whole. If you provide 12 specific rules the AI cannot break plus 16 writing samples, the output is roughly five times better. After 100 such feedback cycles the output is perfectly pattern-matched to the desired style, and those 100 cycles that would take 18 months with a human employee take approximately 100 minutes with an AI agent.

_from how_to_win_with_ai_in_2026_9q5ojtkqsBs.txt_

nodes.label: Hormozi recounts a Brian Johnson (Blueprint longevity company founder) analogy: …
nodes.description:
**Example:** Hormozi recounts a Brian Johnson (Blueprint longevity company founder) analogy: humans have progressively become better swimmers, moving from lap pools to open ocean. But the coming AI shift is not a bigger wave in the same medium; it is a phase shift from water to gas. A perfect swimmer still cannot swim when the water has evaporated. The analogy is meant to convey that AI represents a fundamental environmental change rather than a skill upgrade, and competitive advantages built for the old environment may not transfer.

_from how_to_win_with_ai_in_2026_9q5ojtkqsBs.txt_

nodes.label: Hormozi uses the AI-generated adult content industry as a leading-indicator exam…
nodes.description:
**Example:** Hormozi uses the AI-generated adult content industry as a leading-indicator example of where AI will eventually penetrate mainstream entertainment and media. He describes businesses generating AI avatar personas, producing automated video content, and deploying chatbots trained on thousands of domain-specific conversations, all without the logistical overhead of managing real people. His argument is explicitly economic rather than normative: whatever the adult content industry adopts first tends to reach mainstream use eventually, and the pattern here is AI-generated personas plus automated conversation at scale.

_from how_to_win_with_ai_in_2026_9q5ojtkqsBs.txt_

nodes.label: Coca-Cola is sold in approximately 12 different retail formats and contexts. A c…
nodes.plugin: Price as Expectation and Quality Frame
nodes.description:
**Example:** Coca-Cola is sold in approximately 12 different retail formats and contexts. A consumer purchasing a cold can from a refrigerated vending machine pays 6-8 times more per unit volume than a consumer buying the same beverage in a room-temperature 2-liter PET bottle from a discount store. The identical product in different packaging and environmental contexts generates radically different willingness-to-pay.

_from how_value_is_built_in_the_mind_i93Qu7dckn4.txt_

nodes.label: Water purchased in a bottle format was rejected by the speaker ('no thanks I'll …
nodes.description:
**Example:** Water purchased in a bottle format was rejected by the speaker ('no thanks I'll buy something else'). The identical or chemically similar water presented in a can format was positively received ('actually this is quite a nice part of my hydration repertoire'). Packaging alone—not the product—drove the difference in acceptance.

_from how_value_is_built_in_the_mind_i93Qu7dckn4.txt_

nodes.label: Alex Hormozi describes how Gym Launch avoided needing ~100 account reps by using…
nodes.description:
**Example:** Alex Hormozi describes how Gym Launch avoided needing ~100 account reps by using a licensing model rather than an agency model. Instead of managing ad accounts for each gym, Gym Launch taught gym owners one simple skill (how to run local ads: drop a pin, target female, go), then licensed monthly ad creative to them. The gym owners ran the ads themselves against pre-tested Gym Launch landing pages. The creative was the consumable they needed every month; the targeting skill was the one-time thing they learned once. This meant Gym Launch's operational team only had to produce and distribute creative, not manage hundreds of individual accounts.

_from how_we_trained_sales_teams_across_thousands_of_gyms_7w1HQAvlLZk.txt_

nodes.label: The questioner's financial advisor sales coaching business illustrates the activ…
nodes.description:
**Example:** The questioner's financial advisor sales coaching business illustrates the activation-churn loop: advisors who do not engage with the coaching and do not learn to close deals churn; advisors who learn the process using the coaching stay. The questioner observed this pattern but was not yet systematically exploiting it to drive avatar selection or activation design. Hormozi identifies this as a solvable problem once the pattern is confirmed.

_from how_we_trained_sales_teams_across_thousands_of_gyms_7w1HQAvlLZk.txt_

nodes.label: Hormozi illustrates avatar selection risk using Gym Launch's own near-mistake: i…
nodes.description:
**Example:** Hormozi illustrates avatar selection risk using Gym Launch's own near-mistake: if Gym Launch had sold to anyone who self-identified as a 'fitness person,' it would have included personal trainers with 10 clients who could not afford meaningful coaching and whose economics never worked. By restricting to gym owners at a minimum business size (quantifiable threshold), Gym Launch ensured it could deploy enough resources per customer to actually get results and charge enough to sustain that deployment.

_from how_we_trained_sales_teams_across_thousands_of_gyms_7w1HQAvlLZk.txt_

nodes.label: Experimental psychologists create delicious cakes using only sugar, flour, and c…
nodes.description:
**Example:** Experimental psychologists create delicious cakes using only sugar, flour, and chocolate that look like feces. Despite rational knowledge that the ingredients are safe and the cake is delicious, people find it extremely difficult to eat because they have an extraordinary amount of instinct telling them not to eat anything that looks like feces. The instinctive rejection overrides the conscious knowledge of safety.

_from huge_limitations_of_the_conscious_mind_marketing_london_mark_VSXjEGu8fNI.txt_

nodes.label: A person at a drunk party instinctively kisses someone they don't even particula…
nodes.description:
**Example:** A person at a drunk party instinctively kisses someone they don't even particularly like. On the way home, rather than acknowledge the impulsive behavior, they consciously construct an elaborate story: their wife doesn't understand them, they're trapped in the marriage, this kiss was justified. The narrative—which feels like it should have preceded the action—was actually fabricated after the behavior as a post-hoc justification.

_from human_being_are_on_autopilot_KRgXM5i7Tew.txt_

nodes.label: Alex Hormozi uses the evolutionary berry-eating scenario to illustrate the mecha…
nodes.description:
**Example:** Alex Hormozi uses the evolutionary berry-eating scenario to illustrate the mechanism of pessimism bias. The ancestor who assumed unknown berries might have upside (and ate them) died if they were poisonous. The ancestor who assumed unknown berries were dangerous and avoided them survived to reproduce. Across thousands of generations, the optimistic risk-takers died, removing their genes, while the cautious pessimists survived and passed on their caution. The result is that the entire surviving human genome is derived from people who systematically over-weighted downside — making pessimism bias not a personal failing but an inherited biological default.

_from humans_overestimate_the_downside_I8YZLBYYMag.txt_

nodes.label: Alex Hormozi describes his own earlier mindset of fear — asking himself what hap…
nodes.description:
**Example:** Alex Hormozi describes his own earlier mindset of fear — asking himself what happens if he does not figure it out — and the realization that the answer is simply to keep trying. He presents this as a first-person experience of the psychological nature of failure: not figuring something out does not end the game, it just produces another iteration. The emotional weight of fear before the attempt was the entire cost; the actual experience of not figuring it out was merely an invitation to try again.

_from humans_overestimate_the_downside_I8YZLBYYMag.txt_

nodes.label: Drew's fence-visualization SaaS (approximately $500K ARR at time of interview) r…
nodes.description:
**Example:** Drew's fence-visualization SaaS (approximately $500K ARR at time of interview) ran a 10-day free trial with credit card attached and cancel-anytime policy. Users who placed a fence visualization in at least one customer's yard within the trial window almost never canceled; users who did not attempt the feature within 10 days churned at a rate that drove an overall 8% monthly churn. Alex Hormozi diagnosed this as a trial incentive gap: the free trial gave no financial reason to attempt the feature, so most trial users never experienced the product's core value and passively churned.

_from i_built_an_app_and_no_one_s_using_it_-Le_gCaW_5c.txt_

nodes.label: Drew reported a $130 cost-per-lead from Facebook instant-form ads, noting that a…
nodes.description:
**Example:** Drew reported a $130 cost-per-lead from Facebook instant-form ads, noting that a particularly strong ad had produced leads at $1.50 each. Alex Hormozi cautioned Drew not to rely on the $1.50 figure and pointed out that the $130 figure itself was likely the cost per trial signup rather than the cost per paying retained customer. With roughly 8 trials converting to 3-4 paying customers, the true CAC was closer to $500, not $130 — a 3-4x understatement that would distort any decision about whether to scale ads.

_from i_built_an_app_and_no_one_s_using_it_-Le_gCaW_5c.txt_

nodes.label: The apartment broker in this conversation ran $2M in revenue in 2022 but had dec…
nodes.description:
**Example:** The apartment broker in this conversation ran $2M in revenue in 2022 but had declined to ~$250K by the time of the conversation. When pressed, he acknowledged the market was much better in 2022 — confirming that some of the revenue decline was external (real estate transaction volume fell sharply). However, Hormozi used this acknowledgment to reinforce that the broker understood the cause yet still felt paralyzed — illustrating the 'between the ears' bottleneck where the founder can explain the problem but still lacks clarity on the morning action.

_from i_feel_stupid_apartment_broker_stuck_at_250k_pEKRblMK-Xg.txt_

nodes.label: The apartment broker described the typical hiring pattern in his industry: bring…
nodes.description:
**Example:** The apartment broker described the typical hiring pattern in his industry: bring in a junior agent, train them as a junior, and 90% burn out within a year — creating a cycle where the founder's training investment yields near-zero retention. Hormozi used this to argue the solution is not more average hires but one exceptional hire ('stud') who has sufficient skill and motivation to stay productive without constant hand-holding.

_from i_feel_stupid_apartment_broker_stuck_at_250k_pEKRblMK-Xg.txt_

nodes.label: The broker admitted he had already attempted one hire, lost money, and described…
nodes.description:
**Example:** The broker admitted he had already attempted one hire, lost money, and described having a 'negative CAC' — meaning the cost of the failed hire exceeded any revenue generated. This is cited as a concrete reason the broker's confidence in hiring is impaired, illustrating why the swamp trap is psychologically as well as financially constraining: a failed first bet makes the second bet feel even larger.

_from i_feel_stupid_apartment_broker_stuck_at_250k_pEKRblMK-Xg.txt_

nodes.label: Alex Hormozi cited Sharran Srivatsaa (referenced by first name as 'Sharron') as …
nodes.description:
**Example:** Alex Hormozi cited Sharran Srivatsaa (referenced by first name as 'Sharron') as a real-world case: Sharran came to the US from India with a thick Indian accent, received feedback that the accent would limit his market access, and deliberately worked to remove it. Hormozi used this as justification for why he felt comfortable giving the same non-politically-correct advice to the India-based physics tutor asking the question.

_from i_m_a_physics_tutor_making_80k_how_do_i_scale_bBm70Ojep80.txt_

nodes.label: The agency founder in this conversation described charging $5K upfront plus $2K-…
nodes.description:
**Example:** The agency founder in this conversation described charging $5K upfront plus $2K-$5K/month to financial advisors, running paid Facebook ads to book appointments, and then noticing that advisors could not convert those appointments. He had three mediocre testimonials and a 10% close rate on qualified prospects. Alex Hormozi used this situation to illustrate that the close rate problem was not primarily a sales skill deficiency but a proof deficit: the founder was relying purely on persuasion with no third-party validation to support the offer.

_from i_m_closing_10_of_my_sales_calls_what_am_i_doing_wrong_tWRrd0ClwjA.txt_

nodes.label: Alex Hormozi described the predictable future of this agency founder in sequenti…
nodes.description:
**Example:** Alex Hormozi described the predictable future of this agency founder in sequential steps: follow the free-work advice, accumulate proof, build a compelling VSL, raise prices, close more clients, watch a disproportionate share hit the bottom line, then notice increasing churn and rising CAC. He illustrated the plateau as ending up at roughly $1.8M top line and $250K bottom line with a churn factory, frustrated by small business owners who cannot execute, and needing to call back for advice on what to do next.

_from i_m_closing_10_of_my_sales_calls_what_am_i_doing_wrong_tWRrd0ClwjA.txt_

nodes.label: Alex Hormozi used the observation about the financial advisor client's inability…
nodes.description:
**Example:** Alex Hormozi used the observation about the financial advisor client's inability to convert booked appointments to illustrate that when serving small business owners as a client-acquisition agency, the vendor absorbs client operational dysfunction as churn. The advisor books calls through the agency's paid ads and AI booking system but cannot close them, meaning the agency's metric (appointments booked) does not translate to client ROI, which drives cancellation regardless of delivery quality.

_from i_m_closing_10_of_my_sales_calls_what_am_i_doing_wrong_tWRrd0ClwjA.txt_

nodes.label: Alex Hormozi referenced Ogilvy as the canonical example of the whale/premium-upm…
nodes.description:
**Example:** Alex Hormozi referenced Ogilvy as the canonical example of the whale/premium-upmarket pole of the agency bifurcation, contrasting it with hypothetical super-cheap-high-volume automated agencies. The point was that the largest agencies in the world have not found a sustainable mid-market position, and this structural fact should inform an early-stage founder's path selection.

_from i_m_closing_10_of_my_sales_calls_what_am_i_doing_wrong_tWRrd0ClwjA.txt_

nodes.label: Easy Dwell (Shemaine's company) buys properties from sellers with low-rate finan…
nodes.description:
**Example:** Easy Dwell (Shemaine's company) buys properties from sellers with low-rate financing (e.g., 2% mortgages via sub-2 or seller-carry structures), then resells them inside an LLC structure to buyers who cannot qualify for traditional financing. Per deal, Easy Dwell collects $25,000 upfront and approximately $800/month over 30-40 years in cash flow. Over two years the company completed 46 acquisitions and sold 30, achieving $3M revenue and $500K profit with a fund-level cash-on-cash return of approximately 60%. Alex Hormozi identified the single binding constraint as deal flow: capital was sufficient, execution was working, but only ~40 deals in two years left the business far below market penetration in Florida.

_from i_m_so_confused_walk_me_through_how_you_make_money_fTV3PbWAfWQ.txt_

nodes.label: Alex Hormozi used the analogy of a wholesale franchise location to break Shemain…
nodes.description:
**Example:** Alex Hormozi used the analogy of a wholesale franchise location to break Shemaine's belief that Easy Dwell had tapped the Florida market. A single franchisee for major wholesale franchises averages $3M/year per location, which is the same revenue Easy Dwell generates across the entire business. Hormozi argued that if Shemaine were doing $200M/year in Florida he might be a recognizable player, but at $3M he is not even a blip on the radar of the state's wholesale ecosystem.

_from i_m_so_confused_walk_me_through_how_you_make_money_fTV3PbWAfWQ.txt_

nodes.label: Hormozi illustrated the vertical integration opportunity by describing the game …
nodes.plugin: Vertical Integration to Capture Full Margin
nodes.description:
**Example:** Hormozi illustrated the vertical integration opportunity by describing the game he likes to play: acquire a wholesaler who has volume, and suddenly you have both (1) the wholesaler's stand-alone operating income and (2) a captive deal pipeline for Easy Dwell's financing model. The wholesaler business works on its own; Easy Dwell's model 'just juices' it. He described this as the wholesale business having a worse monetization vehicle than Easy Dwell, so Easy Dwell would be acquiring volume at below its own monetization ceiling.

_from i_m_so_confused_walk_me_through_how_you_make_money_fTV3PbWAfWQ.txt_
